In 1950, this taxpayer paid $964 a year in federal taxes alone. In 1966-and this includes federal and provincial taxes in all provinces except Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Quebec-he paid $863. As a result of the tax changes now proposed he will be paying $958 a year. So there really has not been much change, though I suggest there has been a great increase in the services which the government has provided during the period between the years I have mentioned.
We have heard it said, particularly by members of the New Democratic party, that the tax increase now proposed is beamed entirely toward the individual and that corporations have not been called upon to take the burden. I have been doing a little research work on this subject and I have taken the trouble to find out what the position is in this country with regard to the distribution of federal taxation between the individual taxpayer and the corporations. I make no defence of corporations, except to say we are bound to recognize, whether we like it or not, that business and industry constitute one of the major segments of our society, investing money, taking risks, producing goods and providing incomes which individual citizens enjoy. All this is responsible for the standard of living we have reached. We cannot afford to kill the goose which lays the golden egg.
Here are figures taken from the Canadian Tax Journal. In the United States in 1963,
22.1	per cent of direct tax revenues came from corporations and 77.9 per cent came from individuals. In Sweden, 9.1 per cent of direct taxes was imposed on corporations and 90.9 on individuals. In the United Kingdom,
18.2	per cent came from corporations and 81.8 per cent from individuals, and in France 11 per cent came from corporations and 89 per cent from individuals. In Canada, Mr. Speaker, 35.4 per cent of direct taxes came from corporations and 64.6 per cent from individuals.
Thus, though it is easy to say that the corporations should be soaked, we must be awfully careful lest we kill the goose which lays the golden eggs.

During the last few years, however, the government has introduced major measures of social reform, such as the Canada assistance plan, the income supplement for the aged, medicare and so on. I personally am proud we have done these things. I think they were long past due. They were badly needed, and there are further measures in this general area of social progress which we should consider in due course.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
At the same time, going back to the opinion expressed a few moments ago, there is an economic base from which all these blessings flow, and we have to protect that base. The time has now come for us to stop and temporarily digest the social reform measures we have passed, so as not to overload the economy. It is time now to turn to the theme and to the priority, and for a short period at least as a government to concentrate our investments into economic development, and let the gross national product grow so that the tax base is increased. Then we can afford to move ahead on other needed measures of -ocial reform.
One of these procedures in investment in economic growth, that of regional economic development, has to take place in a much more comprehensive form than exists presently. One can look at the growth of certain sections of the country and see how quickly they are expanding and then turn to other sections and see how slowly their rate of growth is proceeding. Something should be done in such a situation. The urban centres such as Toronto and Montreal-and we could name others-are pyramiding development in their own areas, while other sections of the country are lagging behind.
In particular the province of Ontario requires close examination in terms of subprovincial regional economic development. Ontario is recognized as a "have" province. The statistics of economic performance in Ontario are standouts, so fas as the country as a whole is concerned. But Ontario is a vast province. It contains many different kinds of regions, and there are many different economic regional activity levels in it. There is a wide disparity between the growth rate in the northern part of the province and the tremendous development taking place in Toronto and the golden horseshoe, extending 27053-334
The Budget-Mr. Andras
down to Niagara, Windsor and back to Toronto.
The situation in that southern area of Ontario-and I say this without any attempt to be facetious or critical-is creating so many problems and demanding so much of the attention of the Ontario government that it simply cannot afford to devote sufficient energy, time, effort and money to many of the other sections of the province in order to plan the kind of development that we want to see take place in those sections. In my opinion many other provinces, classified as "have not" provinces, have co-operated a great deal more than Ontario with the federal governmment, particularly through ARDA programs, in seeking stimulation for the economies of their various areas. In this respect I am thinking of provinces like Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Manitoba! I speak with particular concern about this matter because of the situation in my constituency and in my area of northwestern Ontario. We would be incorrect if we were to describe this as a disaster area. Up to the present time we have continued to enjoy reasonable levels of employment, but it is a slow growth area.
With this thought in mind, some 18 months ago I made a number of specific recommendations for the framework of an economic development plan for the area. I negotiated these recommendations with the federal government. The response was encouraging, and I got written approval form the minister of forestry (Mr. Sauve) that ARDA, under the federal administration, would assist in financing the kind of research that had to go into it. Simultaneously with these negotiations with the federal government, I spoke with many people at Queen's Park and in the Ontario government. While the approval came from the federal government many months ago, apparently I have not been a good enough spokesman to move the Ontario government to any action whatever. I say this in a non-partisan way because in the province of Manitoba, which enjoys a Conservative government, as does Ontario, the exact opposite has been the case.

I think that for some long time to come the Ontario provincial government is going to be preoccupied with the demands and the problems of southern Ontario, so that it will not be able to turn much attention to the areas of northern Ontario which demand planning and development.
Some of us, members of different parties in this house, have recently talked to Mr. Kier-ans of Sudbury. I had a most interesting discussion with him a few days ago regarding his proposal for the establishment of an institute for northern development. I told him that I would prefer that it be called an institute for regional development. I do not think that stress on the word north is what we need now. I believe we need a real study into the formation of a national program for regional economic development, whether that development be in the north, south, west or east. This again brings up juridictional problems, the kind of problems I have faced in my negotiations with the Ontario government, which is responsible for regional subprovincial economic development. It seems to me that basically such development is the responsibility of the provincial government and that the federal government can assist only if it is invited to participate. Most certainly this is the view that Queen s Park is taking. Something has to happen to get these areas going which do not enjoy the same rate of growth as the six or seven very affluent areas of the country. I believe that during the discussions next month in the federal-provincial conference, which basically will discuss federal-provincial relations, this matter of regional economic development should 

be placed on the agenda and thoroughly discussed in order that jealousies and jurisdictional problems and other impediments can be removed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this house will be called upon very shortly to vote on the amendment, the motion of non-confidence moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), as our response to the budget message delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). My purpose in participating in the debate at this stage is to review the situation of the country in the context of that amendment and to endeavour to show that every branch of the amendment is justified, and that it should command the support of the house as a serious condemnation of the government, and I say a serious condemnation of the government in the full realization of the implication of those words if the amendment should carry. I hope the amendment will carry because in my view it is in the interest of the country that it should carry and that the government should be forced to resign.
In the amendment now before the house there will be recognized to be three phases. The first is the accusation that the government has created the situation, the mess, to which this budget and the resolutions dependent upon it are supposed to be the response; that is, that the government is responsible for the situation which has brought about this budget. The second phase of the amendment is that the answer of the government is completely inadequate. Their answer is to impose taxes-to increase taxes-which is a completely inadequate response and in no way at all meets the situation which they in fact have created. The third accusation in the amendment is that the taxes-the very measure now proposed by the government-are not only unnecessarily burdensome but may themselves actually aggravate the inflationary condition to which they are supposed to be the answer.
Those are the three branches of the amendment. I should like to develop each one in detail in order to show that they are justified and should indeed command the
December 11, 1967

support of every responsible member in this house.
I shall deal first with the accusation of mismanagement and vacillation. Well, sir, it seems to me that it should not be necessary to advance too much detail in this regard. The fact is that in this year we have had two diametrically opposed budgets. Nothing can more clearly prove the charge of mismanagement and vacillation. There has been a complete change in the government's position between the budget brought down in June and the budget presented to the house within the last two weeks.
I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) says the reason he brought down a second budget is because the circumstances have changed. I say to him that his statement is completely inaccurate and amounts to a gross misrepresentation. The reason he brought down the second budget was not because the circumstances have changed but because the government has grossly overspent and therefore has to impose tax burdens upon the country in order to meet its bills. By its overspending it has dried up the capital markets. The Minister of Finance realizes they are no lower available to him. Therefore, he had to introduce a budget to raise more revenues to pay his bills.
This is not a change in circumstances, because that overspending was the deliberate result of the minister's first budget. In his first budget and in the estimates for 1967-68 which he presented in this house he deliberately forecast expenditures in the sum of $9.5 billion to $10 billion in this fiscal year. That was not an accident. Except in so far as the minister was unable to restrain his colleagues, that was his deliberate purpose. He budgeted indeed at that time for a deficit in the order of $750 million, three quarters of a billion. He had to introduce his second budget, the one we are dealing with, because he found he could not get the money to meet the level of expenditures he himself had imposed upon the country. There is no change of circumstances. This is a budget, a measure of taxation increases, made necessary by the minister's fiscal mismanagement.
There is in addition this feature about his budget: The minister has presented it as an anti-inflationary budget, as an instrument which he tries to pretend is good fiscal management in responding to changed circumstances. Sir, this is not an anti-inflationary budget: It is a revenue raising budget pure and simple. It is a budget to raise the revenues the government now finds it needs in

The Budget-Mr. Fulton order to meet its own grossly inflated spending programs. It is not a management budget. This collection of individuals opposite making up the cabinet has never had the ability to manage. But, sir, even if they ever had it, they have now lost that ability; they have piddled it away. Even if these individuals have now lost it by their own mismanagement.
Second, I should like to demonstrate conclusively that it is in fact the over-expenditure by this government which has created the situation with which we are now faced. Let us look at a few of the figures which are relevant in this connection. Since the 1963-64 fiscal year when this government assumed responsibility-I will not say power, because they have never been able to exercise power since they assumed responsibility-the levels of federal government spending have increased by some 65 per cent. In this period of just over four years the level of civil service employment has increased at a record pace.
I realize that it is not a valid criticism just to talk about the increase in the number of civil servants or the increase in the amount of their salaries; one must ask: What value is the country receiving for these increases? I defy any member of this house to tell me that the 65 per cent increase in federal spending and the record increase in federal payrolls has been matched by a corresponding increase in service to the country.
All that has been happening is gross overinflation in civil service payrolls and in government spending authorizations.
In support of that statement I should like to cite a Canadian Press dispatch which appeared in the Vancouver Sun-which is not a paper favourable to the party to which I have the honour to belong-of October 19, 1967. In examining the figures the Vancouver Sun reports as follows:
Civil service employment has been creeping up steadily from its wartime peak of 116,000 in 1945.
But it didn't really start to surge until the start of 1965. Since then it has increased by an astonishing 9 per cent.
Then a little later on the report continues:
The budget estimate for civil service payrolls in the current fiscal year is $1.3 billion, an increase of 44 per cent in three years.
It will take the combined personal income tax revenues from Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, Winnipeg and Hamilton to cover the bill.
Most of the staff increases can be traced to an unprecedented upsurge in the creation of new departments, agencies and programs.
December 11, 19S7

The Budget-Mr. Fulton That is a statement of the facts-an unprecedented upsurge in the creation of. new departments, agencies and programs unmatched by any increase in real services or real production for the people of Canada.
But when faced with this criticism-these facts-unfortunately the minister, on behalf of the government, instead of recognizing that the government is at least partly to blame for the inflationary pressures, indulges in a form of political finger pointing, as thought he were a small boy saying, "Yah, you too."
If we could see on the part of this government any readiness to recognize its responsibility for creating, or contributing to, the situation or to respond by mending their ways, then one might have to be more temperate or more moderate, if you like, in the criticism we make; but unfortunately one sees the reaction only of small politicians, because when faced with this statement of fact by the Leader of the Opposition the other day, what was the response of the Minister of Finance? His reply was typical of a government which is more obsessed with political justifications than with the responsibilities to the job it has to do.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
So the Minister of Finance contented himself by saying that the record of the present Leader of the Opposition, as premier of Nova Scotia, had been even worse than the record of the present government. His only answer was to point to the situation in Nova Scotia, Let me read from page 5215 of Hansard for December 8, where the minister is reported as having said:
Between the years 1956 and 1966, a period when my hon. friend occupied the position oi premier of that province, the public service of Nova Scotia, those in government employment, rose from approximately 10,300 to 14,419. This is an increase of just under 40 per cent. In the same period the number of civil servants in Canada rose from 336,000 to 361,000 approximately. This is an increase of 311st about 7 per cent. These are comparisons that I think should be brought to the attention of the house.
Well, Mr. Speaker, may I ask what kind of a minister is this and what kind of an inept answer is that? If it were an answer at all, it is still a completely political answer. Even if the comparison were apt or fair, to say to somebody else that your record is bad, therefore mine is good, is not an answer. This does not justify to the slightest degree the lack of responsibility and fiscal restraint on the part of this government.


And of course, the situations are not comparable, so the minister's reply is not even apt in that respect. One must look at the question in the light of the starting points. It was recognized by our party and by the government which we formed in the years between 1957 and 1963 that there was a disparity between the levels of the economy and of government services as between the maritime areas and the rest of Canada. We as a responsible federal government deliberately encouraged and made it possible for the government of Nova Socia, as well as other maritime governments, to increase the level of their government services.
As a measure of federal government assistance we introduced the Atlantic Development Grants Act, and it was in response to that act that the government of Nova Socia and the governments of other Atlantic areas were encouraged to increase the numbers of their federal civil servants and the number of government services they could render to their people. That increase in Nova Scotia civil service was the deliberate result of a deliberate federal policy, and all that the Minister of Finance has said provides a record of the beneficial results of the deliberate, responsible, intelligent and effective federal government policy of those days.
Again in respect of this matter of mismanagement and vacillation, it becomes quite apparent that in spite of what the government has been saying, it realizes that it is overspending and that this overspending is one of the major contributory factors to the inflationary trend from which the country suffers today. Let me now prove this point.
The government deliberately estimated for a budgetary deficit of $750 million this fiscal year. That estimate has now risen, as a result of the supplementary estimates, to over $800 million. The sorry fact is that the government really does nothing about this present situation. It has done nothing about one of the root causes of the inflationary trend, that is, its own gross overspending. It has done nothing about its overspending for this year.
But in answer to the criticism-which he recognizes in his heart is valid-the minister makes the pretence of doing something by discussing next year's projected expenditures. So, we have an exercise by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) a couple of nights ago when he listed a long and exhaustive mass of detail about possible reductions in next year's spending programs. Of course
December 11, 1S67

this was nothing more than an exercise in a shallow pretence. No single phrase of that minister's speech can demonstrate this shallow pretence more clearly than one to be found at page 13 of the advance text of his speech which was distributed to us. He said:
We are now approaching the final stages of the 1968-69 estimates exercise.
That is all this great build-up, fanfare and publicity about the huge saving the government is going to make next year amounts to-nothing more than an exercise. It is just that-an annual exercise in the process of the review by the Treasury Board in its regular course of paring the departments' official submissions down to that which comes out in the blue book of official estimates.
A true measure of the folly and the fantasy to which we were subjected last week is shown by some of the so-called savings that are to be made. There was a list of some four or five pages presented. Let me give you some choice examples of these great savings to be made on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada. At page 17 of the advance text we are told:
The special planning secretariat within the Privy Council office will be disbanded: henceforth its essential functions in the field of co-ordination of social development programs will be carried as part of the normal operations of the cabinet secretariat.
We are then left with this disturbing question: If this is part of the normal operations of the cabinet secretariat, why on earth was this put elsewhere in the first place? How in heaven's name does this return to normal lead to a real saving?
Another example is this:
Financial provision for the Company of Young Canadians will be reduced by 20 per cent from the $2.4 million budgeted for the current year.
I am sure the people of Canada will welcome that huge saving of 20 per cent of $2.4 million budgeted for the Company of Young Canadians. I go no further, but the implication is obvious.
The next example appears on page 19 of this advanced text. It states:
Provision for staff travel throughout the public service is being cut by a full 10 per cent from departmental requirements as submitted in estimates for the year 1968-69.
Bully for you boys. But how much was submitted for last year? Departmental travel possibilities for next year is being cut by 10 per cent. I am sure the Canadian people can

The Budget-Mr. Fulton be expected to cheer about this real saving which will represent such hypothetical hardship to the government. Surely this is a nonsensical statement.
This is the vein in which these examples can be repeated. For instance, we are told the external affairs department planned to open two new diplomatic missions abroad in 196869, and trade and commerce planned to open three new posts. These plans are to be deferred as a reuult of the hard and ruthless decision of this government.
Again, according to the speech of the Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board there will be a slowdown in the plans for headquarters buildings for three departments in Ottawa, namely external affairs, transport and national defence. These are not projects already in existence, they represent deferments and great savings in respect of things that might never have happened anyway. Is it not amazing that the three departmental headquarters to be deferred do not include the department headquarters of the minister? It is well known that these plans included the construction of an elaborate and expensive new headquarters building for the Department of National Revenue. One might have thought that when the minister was asking for these great sacrifices on the part of his colleagues he would have been willing to set a practical example by cutting out his own departmental headquarters. But no, the measure of the government's seriousness in this program is contained in the words of the minister to his colleagues when he said "you must defer your plans, but mine of course are essential". So the Canadian people are going to pay for a new national revenue headquarters building but are invited to rejoice in the amount of these other so-called savings.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I could go on, but perhaps this is the peach of them all. I refer to item No. 38 on page 25 of the advance text of the statement of the Minister of National Revenue, which reads as follows:
The Transport Department has also been asked to defer all reconstruction and improvement work on the Rideau and Trent canal systems other than that which is absolutely necessary to maintain the systems in proper operating condition.
What else could the expenditures properly have been expected to cover other than to
December 11, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Fulton maintain the canal system in proper operating condition? But that is the nature of the whole fantastic operation, namely raising to the level of a virtue the cutting out of frills and reducing expenditures to what is necessary to maintain the government service in proper operating condition. I do not think I need say more to demonstrate the fantasy and futility of the operation to which this parliament and the country has been subjected by the government.
But what about priorities? What has been done while this exercise in futility has been going on? What has been done to produce a proper program of priorities? Nothing.
The Minister of Finance told us earlier in the session that the true measure of priorities is not what you keep at the top but what you cut off at the bottom. Let us look at this bottom-lopping exercise. What has the government kept at the top and cut off at the bottom? At the top they have kept medicare, and the Minister of Finance refuses to exercise his proper responsibility, and indulges in disgraceful political jockeying with the provincial finance ministers on whom he tries to fob off the responsibility for the program regardless of whether it should go through or not. He has stated officially that medicare remains the top priority program of the present government. But what does he cut off at the bottom? He cuts off at the bottom increases for superannuated federal civil servants who are in need of assistance who need help both from parliament and from the country. This is the measure of the minister's seriousness when he speaks about priorities and about lopping off expenditures at the bottom.

No, Mr. Speaker, I have only a few minutes left in which to complete my expose. The minister has made two speeches already. Perhaps he will make a third one and really answer the serious criticism with which he is faced. He will not do so by asking questions. All he will do is to ask: "What is your stand on medicare?" Our stand on medicare is on the record. We moved a series of amendments when the bill was being debated in the house in which we clearly indicated the kind of medicare program that should be established, and we would accept our responsibility in that regard.


Next, Mr. Speaker, when it becomes apparent that the government is merely indulging in an exercise of futility with respect to this so-called paring of next years projected expenditures, and when they are asked what they intend to do about their current overexpenditures which are contributing so greatly to inflation, they say: "We cannot reduce current expenditures", and they distort the words of the Leader of the Opposition in support of their own futile arguments. We have heard the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board attempt to distort what the Leader of the Opposition had said. They say: "No government can reduce current expenditure programs".
Of course they cannot do so when they are so pusillanimous about it. But if they were really determined to meet their responsibility and to get the country out of the mess into which their programs and their lack of management have landed it, they could and they would reduce the current expenditure programs. Let me give the minister an example of when it was done and when the federal government accepted its responsibility, grappled with the situation, and in fact reduced the current spending programs in the midst of the fiscal year.
It was not pleasant. All my colleagues here who were in the cabinet and those who were our supporters in the party will recall how unpleasant and how difficult it was. But we did it in 1962.

These actions were the basis for the greatest continuing expansion of the Canadian economy that has ever been known.

speechtext:
The fact is that these responsible actions, so different from the actions of the present government, laid the basis for the longest and most uninterrupted economic expansion in the history of the country. I do not only rely on my own words. Let me quote the words of the governor of the Bank of Canada who in his recent speech in Winnipeg verified what I have been saying. I quote the following from page 1 of the text of his speech:
To provide some perspective for my later remarks, I would like to take a brief backward glance at the great economic gains this country has achieved in recent years. We are now well into our seventh year of virtually uninterrupted economic expansion.
If we take away seven from 1967 it will take us back to 1960 or 1961 when the virtually uninterrupted economic expansion began.
Further, the Minister of Finance himself, in moments of frankness, gave credit to the
The Budget-Mr. Fulton same policies for having started the trend. At page seven of the "Economic Review for 1966" which he presented in his white paper on June 1, 1967, he stated:
The generally well balanced nature of Canada's economic progress during the years 1961 to 1965 was a notable feature of that period.
Then, in the "Economic Review for 1965", he said:
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
The 1965 advance in output was a continuation of the expansion which began in early 1961 and which has become the longest in Canadian history.
So, there are the facts. When a government accepts its responsibility to manage the economy, when it has the room and gumption left to exercise some management, then it can and does take measures which will put the economy back on an even keel which will once again permit advance and progress. But when a government fails, as this government has failed, to accept this responsibility, when it tries to pretend to the Canadian people that the responsibility belongs to the opposition because the opposition does not give the government a blueprint as to precisely what it should do, we see the measure of the situation with which we are confronted. We have a government here which has created a mess, and to which it now asks this parliament and the country to respond by enacting measures which are inappropriate, by enacting measures which will lay the greatest burden on those least able to bear it, the average taxpayer. This is what the minister's tax proposals will do.
This government has introduced budget proposals which, far from alleviating the inflationary pressures to which it is supposed to respond, will in fact be most likely to fan the fires of those inflationary pressure. There can be no doubt that a 5 per cent average surtax on income tax across the board will bear most heavily on those least able to bear it. There can be no doubt a 5 per cent surcharge on income tax across the board will be followed by further demands for increased wages, and rightly so. I am not condemning those who will make these demands. They will be faced with increases in costs, of course, and they will make demands. What could be more natural or more proper?

Faced with this situation tor which the government is itself is largely responsible, which has brought about the necessity tor these budgetary proposals, but with the clear evidence that the budgetary measures the government proposes will not solve but will rather aggravate the situation which they have created, I appeal to responsible members on all sides of this house to accept their responsibility and face facts. The fact is, and their responsibility is, that we will not get this country back on an even keel until we face the first necessity for accomplishing that, namely removing this government from office.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity of saying a few words about our present economic situation, which is not only quite complex, but also seriously affected and not at all flourishing.
When we came to this house, in 1962, the Liberals, who were in the opposition at the time, were voicing the same demands and acting the same way as the Tories today.
At the time, the government was blamed for all sorts of things. It was accused of failing to take its responsibilities, of accumulating deficit after deficit, of being unable to balance the budget. It was held responsible for the inflation and general imbalance that were rampant across the country. Yet Liberals were sitting where the Conservatives now sit.
In 1967, the Conservatives sit in the opposition and blame the Liberals, but none of them suggests a real solution to the problem. None of them speaks in terms of truth, in concrete terms; none of them places himself at the level of concrete truths, of Canadian physical realities.
That political situation exists since confederation. Governments have changed from Liberal to Conservative and from Conservative to Liberal, but the situation has always been the same: always the same recommendations and the same protests. In fact, nothing has changed; the two old political parties have never changed anything in the economy. The financial economy of the nation, old as the world, has never been reformed. It has always led to the same results, either under the Liberals or under the Conservatives.

The fight is still going on; non-confidence motions are moved against the government. The Conservatives would like the present government to resign in order to replace it, but they do not have a better solution to offer.
As far as the New Democratic party is concerned, it advocates planning as the panacea for all the ills of the world but, Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary library is overflowing with treatises on planning and not one tenth of those plans have ever been successfully implemented because there was not enough money to finance them. Plans are plentiful but not money to implement them. As long as we lag behind the realities, as long as we fail to deal with the economic situation while taking them into account, we will get the same results.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, it is much easier to make Canadians accept the deficit and the tax increases by dividing the budget into three parts, because it seems that half-measures or quarter-measures are easier to accept. When the Conservative party was in power, the budget was divided into two. Now, it is being divided into three; a third part has been added to it, but that does not help the situation.
The present tax increases will hit Canadians harder than before and I would even say that these measures are robbing Canadians of their purchasing power, which is already limited. These measures are a way of controlling people. They restrict credit and make prices go up. Therefore, this will be worse than the 1929 depression, when there was a restriction of credit accompanied by a slump in prices. These tax increases by the gover-ment mean that the people are being robbed always more, increasingly controlled by the civil authorities and subjected to a greater surveillance. It means that families and individuals will be poorer. It means a form of Slavery imposed by the state. Whether the country is administered by the Grits or the Tories, it is always slavery.
We have never enjoyed a system bringing stability in Canada. We had crises, depressions, tax increases, reductions of the purchasing power, the burden being put on the shoulders of the taxpayers who cannot even provide for themselves, inflation and deflation, but stability, never.
Progress has to be paid by those who have realized it, by favouring those who produce
December 11, 1967

money. Financial exchange is accepted blindly. There are people occupying responsible positions who will never admit being a little irresponsible. Yet, on many occasions, their reasoning and conclusions have no factual basis. In other words, they are in complete contradiction with the facts before their eyes, especially with respect to economic policies. That kind of irresponsibility seems to develop among progressive countries as the population imagine that they are becoming more civilized and boast that their standard of living is improving. They lose the sense of reality which is only regained when circumstances drive them away from civilization or when they are the victims of major disasters.
Mr. Speaker, in the midst of our present civilization which is offering us an abundance of all kinds, we note that in our country and in our cities where stores are full of products, our fellow-citizens and the hon. Minister of Finance are thinking and acting solely in terms of money. If however, money is scarce, they are condemned to die in the presence of abundance which is in fact quite visible.
And so, Canada, a country which is developing magnificently, with a wealth in production and a great potential, subjects the pace of its production, as well as the standard of living of its citizens, to the fluctuations of the financial credit it may be granted or refused, that may be rationed or lavished, not by its producers, but according to the whims of the men or institutions which have taken control.
If the country were drawn into a war which would force it to devote a good part of its productive capacity to supplying machines of destruction or the flower of its manhood to kill or be killed, the present government would immediately cease to impose credit restrictions and would refuse to stop for lack of money. It would then think in terms of realities, of arms and materials. It would no longer want to be hampered by financial nonsense.
